newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end higher, led by gold jump.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end higher, led by gold jump.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended higher Thursday, led by a jump in gold prices on fund, trade house, and commission house buying, on good volume, traders said.

"Gold has been technically oversold for sometime now, and open interest on COMEX is way, way up, so a short covering rally would not be surprising," Credit Lyonnais Rouse's New York chief bullion dealer, Scott Mehlman, said.

"Today's move appeared to be triggered by breaches of minor resistance around $321.00 and then $324.00, but August gold still has to get back up through major resistance around $325.00 to set off a big rally," he said.
"In the meantime, the brave will sell it again and probably be rewarded, but it won't be easy tomorrow," he said.
COMEX August gold ended up $6.00 at $324.70 an ounce, its highest level in ten days, with total COMEX gold volume estimated at 60,000 lots.
COMEX floor traders said the John. W. Henry & Co managed futures funds were seen leading the shortcovering in COMEX gold Thursday.

On Monday this week, the Wall Street Journal reported that John W. Henry's $1.2 billion Financial and Metals portfolio, which had lost six percent for the year by the end of June, now positive returns of seven percent year-to-date, partly as a result of a huge short position in gold.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $323.50/00, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $319.40 and the New York close Wednesday around $317.80/30.

Implied lease rates for gold eased to around 2.45 percent for one month Thursday, down from 2.60 percent Wednesday, but are still at their highest levels since January, as central bank gold lending finances hedge fund short selling.

Gold fixed at a 12 year low last week at $315.75 in London, in the wake of news of a sale of 167 tonnes of gold by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), which encouraged massive amounts of extra short selling by hedge funds, analysts said.
COMEX gold open interest rose a further 4,699 lots to 222,069 contracts Wednesday, the highest level in 18 months.

Fund short positions in COMEX gold now amount to almost 300 tonnes (9.65 million ounces), analysts said, equivalent to about half South Africa's annual output, and more than twice as big as the fund short positions on COMEX in 1993, just before gold began a rally to seven year highs in early 1996.

But the COMEX position limit is 750,000 ounces (7,500 contracts), so hedge funds use the OTC market to add extra positions, as daily average turnover in the bullion market is around 1,000 tonnes (32.4 million ounces) a day, according to the London Bullion Market Association.

As a result, hedge fund OTC market short positions may currently be as high as 2,000 tonnes, or roughly equivalent to all outstanding producer hedges, and an amount greater than the sum of all published net central bank sales in the last ten years, one analyst said.

Last Sunday South African newspaper, the "Financial Mail" said George Soros was widely believed to be among the fund managers shorting gold, though a Soros spokesman refused to comment. Soros's Quantum Fund manages $15 billion in assets.
But gold's supply/demand fundamentals are improving, with up to 60 percent of world gold mines now producing below total production costs, after gold slide to 12 year lows, analysts said.

Unlike in 1985 though, when gold prices fell to $285 an ounce, the gap between mine supply and fabricator demand for jewellery and industrial uses is now 500 to 1,000 tonnes a year (15-30 million ounces).

COMEX September silver ended up 6.00 cents at $4.245 an ounce, after breaking down out of its $4.40-4.24 range of the past week on Wednesday. In London Thursday morning silver fixed at $4.2235 an ounce, a new three year low.
NYMEX platinum group metal (PGM) futures ended higher also, recovering from two month lows seen in the past week.
NYMEX October platinum closed up $1.50 an ounce at $393.70, while NYMEX September palladium ended up $2.70 at $160.35.
Russian shipments of palladium to Japan resumed this week after a six month suspension, but problems appear to be developing with shipments of platinum, which have not arrived yet, traders said.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
